questions.stem: Reviewers conceded that the physics was inherently {1} — no exposition, however skilled, could make Hawking radiation easy — but they faulted the author nonetheless for {2} matters further with a private notation that no working physicist had ever adopted.
questions.explanation: The dash-clause says no exposition could make the material easy, so the first blank must mean deep and hard to grasp: abstruse. "Intelligible" reverses that, and "derivative" (unoriginal) says nothing about difficulty. The second blank follows "faulted," so it must name a fault the author added on top of an already hard subject — obfuscating; elucidating would be a virtue, and emulating has no object here.

questions.stem: When the main turbine failed the ship did not go dark: an {1} generator, idle until that moment but fully capable, took up the entire electrical load — something the merely {2} equipment stowed beside it, built for cleaning and monitoring, could never have done.
questions.explanation: The generator is held in reserve yet strong enough to carry the whole load, which is exactly auxiliary — subordinate in rank, not in capability; vestigial and ornamental would deny it any working function. The contrasted equipment does menial support work (cleaning, monitoring), so it is ancillary, peripheral rather than merely secondary; "primary" and "indispensable" would destroy the contrast the sentence is built on.

questions.stem: Unable to fund a second full-time crew, the county relied each fire season on {1} companies of trained volunteers, fully equipped to fight a blaze unaided but called out only when the regular stations were stretched.
questions.explanation: The volunteers are competent enough to fight a fire on their own but are held back until the regulars are overstretched — backup support, which auxiliary and reserve both express, yielding the same sentence. Ancillary would make them peripheral hangers-on rather than firefighters, and subordinate speaks only to rank; itinerant and clandestine fit the grammar but assert travel and secrecy the sentence never mentions.

questions.stem: The cartoonist's power lay in {1} rather than invention: the minister's jaw really was that heavy, and precisely because every reader could recognize the feature, the {2} proved impossible to shrug off.
questions.explanation: "Rather than invention" and "really was that heavy" force the first blank toward enlarging something genuinely present: amplification; fabrication is the invention the sentence rules out, and emulation would mean imitating admiringly. The finished drawing is therefore a caricature, which exaggerates real features — a pastiche merely assembles borrowed styles, and an encomium is praise, which nobody would need to shrug off.

questions.stem: Defenders of the novel insisted that its financier was not a portrait but a {1}: every trait the character displayed the living man had displayed too, only swollen to three times its natural size.
questions.explanation: The colon defines the term precisely: nothing is invented, real traits are simply inflated, which is the method a caricature names. Parody imitates a style rather than a person's features, pastiche assembles borrowings, and fabrication would mean the traits were made up, which the sentence denies; an effigy is a figure made to be burned or displayed, not a distorted likeness in prose.

questions.stem: The prosecutor argued that the pattern of crimes revealed not momentary weakness but settled {1}: a character in which cruelty met no internal resistance whatever.
questions.explanation: The colon specifies wickedness lodged permanently in the character rather than a lapse, which depravity and turpitude both name, producing equivalent sentences. Decadence would describe self-indulgent decline, not cruelty without restraint, and negligence describes carelessness rather than wickedness; cupidity narrows the vice to greed, and contrition would make the defendant remorseful, contradicting the clause.

questions.stem: The memoirist takes care not to confuse categories: the thefts of his own adolescence he records as {1}, embarrassing but easily forgiven, whereas his uncle's methodical cruelty toward the household servants he offers as evidence of settled {2}.
questions.explanation: "Embarrassing but easily forgiven" fixes the first blank at the trivial end of the scale — peccadilloes; atrocities and felonies are far too grave to be shrugged off that way. Methodical cruelty set against those small lapses demands the heaviest term available, depravity; indiscretion belongs with the adolescent thefts, and eccentricity registers oddity rather than moral rot.

rejects.problem: "Abstruse" is an equally defensible fit. The intended logic is presumably that "the subject matter was identical" removes content-difficulty explanations (esoteric, arcane, abstruse all point to inherently deep or specialized content), leaving a defect of expression — "obscure," the direct antonym of "clarity." But that distinction is far too fine to be decisive: "abstruse prose/papers" is standard idiomatic usage for writing that is hard to follow regardless of whether the underlying topic is deep, and the sentence's evidence (students needing a commentary to follow the argument) is fully satisfied by "abstruse." "Arcane" is also arguably usable in its loose sense of "impenetrable." Only "prolix" (merely verbose) and "esoteric" (restricted to initiates — contradicted by the identical-subject clause) are cleanly excluded. A well-prepared test-taker could reasonably choose "abstruse" and be marked wrong, so the item is not usable as written; it needs a clue that pins the fault to the writing itself (e.g. "so tangled and elliptical") or the removal of "abstruse"/"arcane" from the option set.
rejects.stem: The subject matter was identical in both cases, yet where his lectures were models of clarity, his published papers were so {1} that even his own doctoral students kept a colleague's commentary at hand in order to follow the argument.
